opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question we've had to think about pretty carefully. Our basic philosophy is that we want engineers to use these tools as much as they find useful. The productivity upside is large enough that, if you start rationing access, you're probably leaving a lot of value on the table. So the default is to make it easy for people to try things, including the newest models and coding agents, without filing a ticket every time.

"Unlimited" doesn't mean "unobserved," though. We track usage the way we'd track any other infrastructure cost: by team, by tool, by workflow. The point isn't to police individuals. It's to understand where the spend is actually going. Most of the time you find a small number of patterns driving most of the cost, like an agent stuck in a loop, or someone running a huge batch job through an expensive frontier model when a smaller model would do just as well. Those are engineering problems, and you fix them the way you'd fix an inefficient query.

The other piece is trying to tie usage to outcomes. Token counts alone don't tell you much. One person might use ten times more than another and be ten times more productive. So we look at things like whether the code gets merged, whether the reviews are useful, and whether people keep coming back to a tool. That tells you which tools are worth investing in and which are just novel.

And honestly, it's an evolving thing. Prices keep dropping, the models keep getting better, and the way people use them changes every few months. So we try not to lock in rigid policies. We keep the guardrails light, watch the data, and adjust. The bigger risk for most companies right now isn't overspending on AI. It's under-adopting it and not learning fast enough how it changes the way your teams work.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I'd frame it is that we never actually tried to "manage" unlimited usage in the sense of rationing it. The philosophy from pretty early on was that we wanted everyone at the company to be using these tools as much as they possibly could, because the people who use them the most end up being the ones who figure out what the tools are actually good for. And that's incredibly valuable to us as a company that's building AI products. We learn a lot from our own engineers hitting the limits of what Claude or Cursor or whatever the tool is can do.

So the first thing is, we just don't put hard caps on it for engineers. If someone is spending a lot on tokens, that's usually a signal that they've found a workflow that works, not that they're wasting money. The cost of a few thousand dollars a month in inference for an engineer is small compared to what that engineer costs, and if it makes them even twenty or thirty percent more productive, it's obviously worth it.

The second thing, and this is where it actually gets interesting, is that we do look at the usage data, but more as a product signal than a cost control. We can see which teams are using agents heavily, which repos get the most agentic edits, where people are building their own harnesses on top of the models. And that tells us a lot about where the friction is. Some of the stuff we've built into the Databricks platform, like the agent evaluation tooling and the way we do governance over model calls, came directly from watching how our own teams were using these things internally and seeing what they struggled with.

The third piece is that we do care a lot about governance in the sense of what data the models can touch. That's different from usage limits. An engineer can call the model as much as they want, but if they're pointing an agent at customer data or production systems, we need the same access controls we'd apply to any human. That's actually the hard problem, and it's the one we think about a lot for customers too. Unlimited usage is easy. Unlimited usage with the right permissions and auditability is the real engineering challenge.

And then honestly, the last thing is, costs are coming down so fast that whatever budget you set today is going to be wrong in six months anyway. So you're better off letting people run and adjusting if something gets truly out of hand, rather than designing elaborate quota systems that'll be obsolete by the time you ship them.

astra-6.text: I think the key is to separate experimentation from production. You want people to have room to try things without worrying about the cost of every request. But you also need visibility into usage and some guardrails, because an automated workflow can consume a lot more than a person chatting with a model. Then, as something becomes a production application, you can ask: What value is it delivering, and can we deliver that value more efficiently? I’d focus on making useful experimentation easy while making the costs understandable.

sol-6.1.text: I think the key is to give people room to experiment while making the costs visible. You don’t want someone to have to ask permission every time they try an idea. But “unlimited” also shouldn’t mean that nobody knows what’s being spent or what value it’s creating. I’d separate exploratory usage from production workloads: keep experimentation easy, and then measure cost, quality, and reliability much more carefully as something scales.
